title: Seller Impersonation and Title Fraud: Why Verification Is Now Part of Every Deal
metaTitle: Seller Impersonation and Title Fraud: Verify Every Deal
metaDescription: Fraudsters have impersonated owners and sold homes they did not own. How agents and property managers can verify owners, vendors and payment details.
excerpt: Fraudsters have impersonated owners and sold homes they did not own. How agents and property managers can verify owners, vendors and payment details.
answer: Fraudsters have learned to impersonate property owners, list homes they do not own and walk away with the proceeds. Similar tactics can target payments to contractors. For Winnipeg agents and property managers, verifying identities and vendors is part of protecting clients: confirm identity, check title, and confirm any banking change by phone using a number you already have.

blocks.x: How seller impersonation fraud works

[Canadian Press reporting](https://building.ca/impersonators-posing-as-homeowners-linked-to-32-fraud-cases-in-ontario-and-b-c/) from January 2023 described mortgage and title fraud, including seller impersonation fraud, involving at least 32 properties in Ontario and British Columbia, with fraudsters posing as owners or tenants. The story described this pattern:
Fraudsters target properties with **low or no mortgages**, and some cases involved **owners living abroad**.
They create **fake identification** in the owner's name.
Sometimes they pay **actors** to list the property and push for a **quick sale**.
In one Ontario case, renters impersonated owners living abroad and sold a home valued at $2.2 million for $1.7 million within two weeks.
Those cases were reported in 2023, in Ontario and B.C. The story does not mention Manitoba, but the same simple checks make sense in any market with absentee-owned rental properties.
The same playbook can target renovation payments

Impersonation can also reach payments for renovation and property work. The [Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre](https://antifraudcentre-centreantifraude.ca/news-nouvelles/2024/2024-02-21-eng.htm) gives the example of a supplier or contractor emailing to request urgent payment to an alternate bank account. Watch for:
**Payment redirection:** a fraudster poses as a contractor and emails new banking details.
**Fake contractors:** someone uses a real company's name to take a deposit.
**Invoice fraud:** fake invoices for work that was never done, sent to property managers handling many projects.
These schemes work because they look routine. A rushed approval or an email that looks legitimate can be all it takes.
Our view: verification is a service, not a hassle

Agents and property managers sometimes worry that extra checks will slow deals or annoy clients. In our view, the opposite is true, and verification now belongs in every deal. Clients want to know their professional is protecting them, and a clear verification process builds trust.
For listings, start with your brokerage's procedures and your regulator's rules, then add:
**Verify identity in person** where possible, or through a trusted verification service.
**Be cautious with absentee owners** who insist on speed, communicate only by email or text, or ask for unusual payment arrangements.
**Check title and ownership history** for recent changes.
**Confirm contact details** independently, not from the documents provided.
For renovation and vendor payments:
**Confirm banking changes by phone** using a number you already have on file, never one in the email.

**Work with renovation companies you can check.** Search the business name in the [Manitoba Companies Office](https://companiesoffice.gov.mb.ca/) registry, ask for references, and ask for past job addresses you can look up in the [City's permit search](https://ppdportal.winnipeg.ca/Permits/PropertyPermitSearch/Start.jsp).

**Check WCB clearance and liability insurance** before work starts. Anyone can pull [a clearance letter](/blog/how-to-check-a-contractors-wcb-clearance-manitoba) from WCB's public Clearance Request System.
**Match invoices to contracts and completed work** before payment.
Choosing vendors you can verify
The simplest protection is to work with vendors you can check. Before you hire a renovation company, look for:
A business name you can confirm in the Companies Office registry.
A WCB clearance you can pull yourself, and a certificate of liability insurance you can confirm with the insurer or broker.
References from recent projects.
Written contracts and itemized invoices.
A clear answer when you ask how they handle any change in payment details.
If a vendor falls short on those, that is a warning sign.
What agents can do
Review your brokerage's identity verification procedures.
Add a fraud-awareness section to your listing presentation.
Share a short vendor-verification checklist with clients who are renovating before a sale.
Keep a list of trusted, verified contractors for clients.
What to watch

Fraud techniques change quickly. Watch for updates from your provincial regulator, the Manitoba Real Estate Association and your brokerage on new schemes and recommended procedures. Ask your title insurer and lenders whether their identity checks add steps to a transaction. Agents who adopt strong verification practices now will be ready for any changes.
A short verification script for agents

Agents can make verification routine with a simple script at the first meeting: "Before we list, our brokerage confirms the identity of every owner and checks the title. It protects you and the buyer. Here's what we need from you." Framing verification as standard practice, not suspicion, keeps the conversation comfortable. Adjust the script to what your brokerage actually does.

For absentee owners, agents should explain that additional steps, such as notarized documents or video verification, may be required, and that these steps protect the owner's property from impersonation.
The bottom line
Verification protects clients, agents and their reputations. Building simple checks into every listing and every vendor relationship is a small effort that can prevent large losses.
